newsitem.title: GERMANY: German online service offers free Internet access.
newsitem.headline: German online service offers free Internet access.

text.p: German Internet surfers are about to discover that there might very well be such a thing as a free lunch in cyberspace.
Germany.Net, a fledgling commercial online service owned by utility RWE AG and Deutsche Bank, said on Thursday that beginning in April it would offer access to the global Internet at no charge.

While surfers will not have to pay a toll on the information superhighway, they might have to put up with a traffic jam or two as their cruise is interrupted by "advertising breaks" that pop up whenever a user changes sites on the World Wide Web.
"Our network in Frankfurt crashed this afternoon because so many people wanted to surf the Internet for free," said Germany.Net managing director Michaela Merz.
Germany.net has around 160,000 registered users who now pay on average between 10 marks ($5.89) and 30 marks to use the service.

But the idea behind the service is to finance usage with advertising rather than subscription fees. It contrasts sharply with the business model of services such as America Online, which supplement subscriber fees with some advertising.
Germany.Net's ad breaks work like this. If a user has viewed 10 to 15 pages on at a Web site, a page of advertising will suddenly pop up that can either be viewed or clicked on to make it go away.
The same procedure is repeated whenever a person leaves a "domain," the main address of a Web site, to go to another.
"We have to be careful. It cannot be too heavy," said Merz, but she added that advertisers were keen to experiment with the model to see if it works.
Germany.net could be the first online service to make such bold use of advertising.

The company also announced that it would cooperate with CompuServe, the U.S. online service, and the Burda publishing group, who would both make some of their online publications available to Germany.Net users.
